title: ResNet – Solving the Depth Problem
description: Exploring ResNet, the residual network that introduced skip connections and made training very deep models possible.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation By 2015, the trend was clear: deeper networks kept winning ImageNet. AlexNet had 8 layers, VGG stretched that to 16 and 19, and GoogLeNet managed 22 with clever modules. But there was a problem: when people tried to go even deeper, training actually got worse. Adding more layers sometimes increased the training error, which didn’t make sense at first. ResNet, introduced by Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research, solved this with a simple but brilliant idea: **residual connections** (a.k.a. skip connections). Instead of forcing each layer to learn a full transformation, they let the layer just learn the difference (the residual). This made training much easier and suddenly networks with 50, 101, or even 152 layers became possible. When I first read about ResNet, it stood out because of how minimal the change was, yet how big the impact turned out to be. A single skip connection redefined the way deep networks were built. ## Model Breakdown The core building block is the **residual block**. Instead of just stacking convolutions, ResNet adds the input back to the output: Input → [Conv → BN → ReLU → Conv → BN] → Add skip connection → ReLU - If input and output dimensions match, the input is added directly. - If they differ, a 1×1 convolution is used to align dimensions. This skip connection allows gradients to flow backward more easily during training, solving the vanishing gradient problem. ### Variants - **ResNet18/34**: Basic blocks with two 3×3 convolutions. - **ResNet50/101/152**: Bottleneck blocks (1×1 → 3×3 → 1×1 convolutions). ResNet152 had 152 layers but was trainable, something that was previously impossible with plain CNNs. It won the 2015 ImageNet competition with a top-5 error rate of 3.57%, surpassing human-level performance. ## Why the Design Choices Matter **Skip connections** These were the magic ingredient. By letting information skip over layers, the network could go much deeper without losing the signal. **Bottleneck design** For deeper versions, the 1×1 convolutions acted like compression layers, reducing computation while still keeping depth. **Normalization** Batch Normalization (BN) was critical here too. Combined with skip connections, it made very deep training stable. --- ## Implementation Notes Here’s a simplified PyTorch version of a basic residual block: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class BasicBlock(nn.Module): def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1): super(BasicBlock, self).__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False) self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) self.shortcut = nn.Sequential() if stride != 1 or in_channels != out_channels: self.shortcut = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False), nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels) ) def forward(self, x): out = self.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x))) out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out)) out += self.shortcut(x) out = self.relu(out) return out ``` What struck me when coding this was how natural the skip connection feels. Adding the input back to the output doesn’t add much complexity but changes training dynamics completely. When I trained a small ResNet on CIFAR10, it converged more reliably than a plain deep CNN of similar size. ## Reflections What I love about ResNet is how small the change was. Just add a shortcut, and suddenly 152-layer networks were trainable. It’s the kind of idea that feels obvious in hindsight but was groundbreaking at the time. The influence of ResNet is everywhere. Modern CNNs, object detectors, and even Transformers all use some form of residual connection. It turned out that this “simple skip” wasn’t just a hack — it became a core design principle. ResNet showed me that sometimes progress in deep learning isn’t about making things more complicated. It’s about making training easier, so depth and scale can do the heavy lifting.
